assessments.hypothesis_name: Distal axon maintenance in long corticospinal tracts
assessments.strategy: The desired perturbation is intracellular: enhance axonal cargo transport and stabilize the actin/microtubule cytoskeleton in the distal axons of cortical upper motor neurons. Biologics cannot act on tubulin post-translational modification, motor-adaptor coupling or microtubule-stabilizing machinery directly, so the only protein-modality routes are indirect: (a) trophic/receptor-agonist biologics that engage a cell-surface receptor on motor neurons and raise axon-maintenance signalling downstream (neurotrophin-family or GDNF-family ligands, IGF-1/mecasermin, agonist antibodies to TrkB or receptor-fusion mimetics); (b) ligand traps or blocking antibodies against extracellular axon-growth inhibitors (anti-Nogo-A/anti-RGMa, anti-LINGO-1) to shift the balance toward axon maintenance; (c) enzyme/protein replacement, which is not applicable because strumpellin is an intracellular multiprotein-complex subunit assembled co-translationally in the cytosol. Route (a)/(b) would be a non-allele-specific, downstream maintenance attempt with no SPG8-specific rationale beyond shared-final-pathway logic. Honest assessment: no biologic executes the stated perturbation, and the cell that must be reached — the cortical Betz/layer-V pyramidal neuron and its lumbar-level axon terminals — is the least accessible target in the body for a systemically dosed protein.
existing_agents: Mecasermin (recombinant IGF-1) — approved for IGF-1 deficiency; tested in ALS/motor neuron disease without benefit, used here only as a precedent for systemic trophic biologics
Anti-Nogo-A antibody (ozanezumab) and anti-RGMa (elezanumab) — clinical-stage CNS axon-protection antibodies, neither tested in HSP
BDNF, CNTF, GDNF recombinant proteins — historical motor-neuron-disease clinical agents, failed largely on delivery/PK/tolerability; tool-grade for this purpose
No agent of any class targets strumpellin or the WASH complex
disease_relevant_cells: Cortical layer V pyramidal (upper motor) neurons, cell bodies in motor cortex
Distal corticospinal axon segments and terminals in cervical/lumbar spinal cord
Patient fibroblasts and iPSC-derived cortical neurons (model cells, accessible in vitro)

delivery_feasibility.target_tissue: Motor cortex and the full length of the corticospinal tract within the spinal cord (CNS, behind the blood-brain and blood-spinal-cord barriers)
delivery_feasibility.target_cell: Upper motor neuron — specifically its distal axon, tens of centimetres from the soma; the therapeutic compartment is intra-axonal cytoskeleton/transport machinery
delivery_feasibility.expected_access: Systemic IgG or recombinant protein reaches ~0.1% of plasma concentration in CNS parenchyma (INFERENCE, general antibody pharmacology), which is below plausible efficacy for a trophic-receptor agonist and gives no access at all to an intracellular cytoskeletal target. Intrathecal dosing distributes along the spinal cord surface but penetrates grey matter poorly and does not reach motor cortex; receptor-mediated BBB shuttles (transferrin-receptor/CD98 bispecifics) are clinically validated for enzyme delivery to CNS in lysosomal disease but deliver cargo into the endolysosomal compartment, not the cytosol, and have not been demonstrated to engage distal axonal cytoskeleton. Degradation-targeting or transport-enhancing protein therapeutics for intracellular neuronal targets remain preclinical with no in vivo CNS precedent (INFERENCE).
delivery_feasibility.major_constraint: Dual barrier failure: the target biology is intracellular/cytoskeletal (no extracellular epitope for a biologic to engage) AND it sits in the least penetrable cellular compartment of the CNS. No existing or near-term biologic platform crosses both barriers.

supporting_evidence.statement: SPG8 pathology is defined as length-dependent degeneration of long corticospinal axons with endosomal/lysosomal trafficking defects, which makes axonal cargo delivery a coherent shared-final-pathway node that is in principle indifferent to the allelic mechanism.

A strumpellin missense variant disrupts actin-dependent endosomal machinery and loses interaction partners, supporting defective actin-based cargo handling upstream of transport failure — i.e. the pathway hypothesis itself is reasonable even if this modality cannot address it.

Receptor-mediated transcytosis shuttles (transferrin-receptor bispecifics) are a genuine, clinically advancing route for getting proteins into CNS parenchyma, so a surface-receptor-agonist biologic is not categorically impossible — it is the intracellular nature of the perturbation that blocks it.

contradictory_evidence.statement: Strumpellin is an obligate subunit of a cytosolic multiprotein (WASH) complex; exogenous protein supplementation cannot assemble into that complex from outside the cell, so enzyme/protein replacement is mechanistically excluded regardless of whether SPG8 is haploinsufficient or dominant-negative.

Axonal transport deficits have not been demonstrated in SPG8 patient neurons, and no validated SPG8 model reproduces spastic paraplegia — so even a deliverable agent would have no in vivo system in which to show target engagement or benefit.

Systemic and intrathecal neurotrophic-factor biologics (BDNF, CNTF, GDNF, IGF-1) have a long record of failure in motor neuron disease, attributable substantially to inadequate CNS/motor-neuron exposure and dose-limiting peripheral effects — the same constraints apply unchanged here.

Relatively early onset and rapid progression in SPG8 mean a downstream maintenance biologic would need presymptomatic chronic CNS dosing, which compounds the immunogenicity and repeat-access problems of intrathecal protein administration.

assessments.biggest_unknown: Whether any extracellular, receptor-accessible node exists between WASH-complex failure and distal axonal dieback in SPG8 neurons. Until a surface-expressed or secreted mediator is identified, there is nothing for a biologic to bind. Secondarily unknown: whether transport failure occurs in SPG8 neurons at all.
assessments.biggest_failure_mode: Target-compartment mismatch, not potency or PK: the perturbation requested (restore intra-axonal transport and cytoskeletal stability) has no extracellular interface, and the one cell that matters — the distal corticospinal axon of a cortical layer-V neuron — is unreachable by any clinically validated protein-delivery platform. A program here would most likely spend its budget producing a well-characterised biologic that demonstrably never engages its intended compartment, with a non-specific trophic agonist read-out that cannot distinguish SPG8 benefit from generic neuroprotection.
assessments.conclusion_note: Recommendation: do not pursue a protein/biologic for this hypothesis. Both failure criteria apply — NO PLAUSIBLE DELIVERY PATH (intracellular axonal cytoskeleton behind the BBB) and effectively NO EXISTING AGENT IDENTIFIED (nothing targets strumpellin/WASH; trophic and anti-Nogo biologics are non-specific and have failed in analogous motor-neuron indications). This hypothesis should be executed by the small-molecule team, which can reach the intra-axonal compartment. Reconsider biologics only if SPG8 work identifies a secreted or surface mediator of distal axonopathy; note also that the dossier's unresolved dominant-negative-vs-haploinsufficiency question (PMID:26572744 recalled, unconfirmed) does not change this conclusion, since neither mechanism is addressable by a protein. Searches for existing agents were not run in this turn; the no-agent finding rests on the mechanistic exclusion above and should be treated as INFERENCE rather than an exhaustive database check.
